Take about one minute each to answer the question on the board."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"When people say they want to be \"normal,\" what do they usually mean? Why might someone feel afraid of not being normal?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think normal means being like everybody else, like having the same clothes and not getting in trouble. People might be afraid of not being normal because kids can make fun of you or leave you out."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Hold on to that idea. Today you will meet a narrator who talks about \"normal\" kids in a very specific way. Your job is to find out what he values, what he fears, and what that might mean for his story."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In our last lesson, Rick Riordan told us myths help people make sense of the world. As I read, ask yourself: what is this myth about our world?"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep Launch to five minutes. Take one or two shares only. Do not let the talk turn into a debate about who is normal. Some students may feel personally touched by this topic, because Percy's story involves learning differences and trouble at school. Frame \"normal\" as an idea the book is exploring, not a label for any student."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students use morphology to build word knowledge for myth language and add this week's vocabulary to their Unit Vocabulary organizers. The ten vocabulary words are then taught in context during the read aloud.","activities":[{"id":"lab-morphology-word-building","title":"Word Building with Myth Roots","minutes":7,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6"],"routine":"Morphology Word-Building Routine","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Watch the word parts on the board. With a partner, build and explain each word. Be ready to say what the word part means and how it changes the whole word."},{"type":"teach","text":"hidden"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Today we study three word parts you will see all unit, because myths are full of them: mort-, -ology, and trans-. Word parts are strategies for figuring out unknown words, and they help us check our thinking."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Write *mort-* on the board. This root comes from Latin and means \"death.\" Say it with me: mort."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"If *mort* means death, what does *mortal* mean? What happens to the meaning when we add the prefix *im-*, which means \"not,\" to make *immortal*?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mortal means something that can die, because mort is death. Immortal has im- in front, so it means not able to die, so living forever. Like the gods in myths."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Right. *Immortal* is one of our vocabulary words. You will see it on page 6. Now write *-ology*. This suffix comes from Greek and means \"the study of.\" *Myth* plus *-ology* gives us *mythology*."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does *mythology* mean? What other school subjects end in *-ology*?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mythology is the study of myths, or a bunch of myths together. Biology is the study of life, and zoology is the study of animals."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Last one: *trans-*. It means \"across\" or \"change.\" Look at *transport* and *transform*. *Port* means \"carry\" and *form* means \"shape.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using the parts, what do *transport* and *transform* mean? Why might *transform* matter in a story about myths and modern kids?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Transport means to carry something across to another place. Transform means to change shape completely. In myths, gods and monsters change shape, and a kid's life could change too."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Per the Unit Outline, do not run a separate context-clue review in this Lab. Context is used during the read aloud (Learning in Action), where students confirm each word in the sentence it appears in. Here, morphology is the strategy. Words that do not contain these parts (envy, frayed, probation, and others) are taught in context during reading. *Dyslexia* can be a quick extension: *dys-* (Greek, \"hard or difficult\") plus *lexia* (\"words\" or \"reading\") gives \"difficulty with words.\" Keep this to about 20 seconds."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners use word parts to build meanings and connect them to home-language knowledge.","sayAsk":"Say each word part aloud with a partner. Ask: Do you know a word in your language that looks like mort-, -ology, or trans-? (Many Spanish words are cognates: mortal, mitología, transformar, transportar, inmortal.) Frames: The word part ___ means ___. So ___ means ___. When I add ___, the word changes to mean ___.","watchFor":"If students guess a meaning without using the word parts, then prompt: \"Which part did you use? What does it mean?\" If students use home-language cognates correctly, then celebrate and have them share with the class. Success: students explain a word's meaning by naming at least one word part and what it means."}]},{"id":"lab-vocab-organizer","title":"Add Words to the Unit Vocabulary Organizer","minutes":3,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6"],"routine":"Vocabulary Organizer","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Open your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. Add these ten words from pp. 1–8: envy, recognize, frayed, expelled, probation, threatened, spawn, detention, immortal, dyslexia. Write each word now. Leave space for a meaning, which you will fill in during the read aloud."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Add *immortal* right now, since we just broke it down. Write: im- (not) + mort (death) = not able to die. The other nine, you will meet in the story. When I pause, you will use the sentence around the word to make a guess, and then we will check it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Ten words is a lot. Only *immortal* gets full morphology treatment here. Treat the others as quick \"guess, check, record\" moments during the read aloud, about 30 seconds each. Words students can usually infer from context (*expelled, detention, threatened*) go fastest, which saves time for *frayed, probation,* and *spawn*."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: copying many words and meanings in a short time","tryThis":"Give a partially filled organizer with the ten words already printed. Have students fill in only the meaning column and a quick sketch or home-language word."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students sort the ten words into \"words about school trouble\" and \"words about feelings or identity,\" and predict which group matters more to the story."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students listen to a fluent read aloud of Chapter 1, pp. 1–8, with teacher think-alouds, and analyze how the narrator's informal, sarcastic word choices create tone and first impressions. Part B: Students cite evidence to make inferences and predictions about whether Percy is being set up as a hero or a problem figure, and begin to name an emerging theme.","activities":[{"id":"lia-read-aloud","title":"Read Aloud and Think-Aloud: pp. 1–8","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","L.6.4"],"routine":"Teacher Read Aloud with Think-Aloud","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"directions","text":"Follow along in your book as your teacher reads aloud. Put a star next to any line where the narrator warns the reader or talks about \"normal\" kids. Underline the ten vocabulary words when you hear them, and jot a guess for each in your organizer."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Model fluent, expressive reading: use a blunt, slightly sarcastic voice, slow down on the warnings, and speed up on the trouble-at-school details. Pause about 5 to 7 times only. Confirm in your edition that the words below fall where the Outline places them (envy and recognize p. 1; frayed and expelled p. 2; probation and threatened p. 3; spawn and detention p. 4; immortal p. 6; dyslexia p. 7)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Think-aloud at the opening: \"The book starts with 'Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood.' That sounds like someone talking right to me, like a friend. And he is telling me to close the book. That is odd. If he really wanted me to stop, why keep writing? He must want me to take this seriously.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Vocabulary in context, *envy* and *recognize* (p. 1). Pause after the narrator says he envies readers who think this is fiction. Say: \"He says he envies normal kids. What could envy mean here? Look at the sentence around it. He wishes he could believe none of this happened, so envy means wishing you had what someone else has.\" Then verify with the dictionary definition on your organizer. Do the same for *recognize*: \"If you recognize yourself in this description, you know it from your own experience.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"*Frayed* (p. 2): Reread the sentence slowly, then ask students what picture the surrounding details paint. Confirm that frayed means worn and coming apart at the edges. *Expelled* (p. 2): Ask what happened to Percy at his past schools, then confirm that expelled means officially forced to leave."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"*Probation* and *threatened* (p. 3): Say: \"Percy is in trouble again. Probation sounds like a last chance. What in the sentence tells us that?\" Confirm that probation is a trial period in which he must behave or face a serious consequence. *Threatened* means warned that something bad will happen. *Spawn* and *detention* (p. 4): Note how *spawn* is used as an insult, and that detention is a school punishment."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"*Immortal* (p. 6): \"We built this one in the Lab. Mort is death, im- means not. So what does immortal mean here?\" Students answer with the meaning and check it in the sentence. *Dyslexia* (p. 7): Briefly confirm the meaning, and note that the narrator treats it as part of who Percy is, not a joke."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word's meaning did you check the most carefully, and what helped you confirm it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I checked probation. At first I thought it was a punishment like detention, but the sentence says he had to behave or he'd get kicked out. So it is like a last chance. The sentence helped me fix my guess."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in following a fast read aloud and in verifying word meanings with context.","sayAsk":"Give students a vocabulary card with a picture or home-language translation for each word before reading. Ask: What does the sentence tell you about ___? Frames: I think ___ means ___ because the sentence says ___. I checked my guess, and ___. The narrator uses the word ___ to show ___.","watchFor":"If students stay silent during pauses, then let them whisper a guess to a partner first. If students memorize the definition but cannot say how the sentence supports it, then prompt: \"Which words around it helped you?\" Success: students record a meaning in their own words and point to a clue in the sentence."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: following the read aloud and tracking the vocabulary","tryThis":"Give students the page numbers for each word in advance so they can find and underline the word before the pause. Allow them to sketch the meaning instead of writing a definition."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain why Riordan might choose *spawn* instead of a more neutral word, and what the word suggests about how others see Percy."}]}]},{"id":"lia-tone-annotation","title":"Tone Through Word Choice","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.1","L.6.4"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"teach","text":"hidden"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Tone is the attitude a narrator shows toward a subject, and it comes from word choice. In Percy's opening, notice casual phrases such as \"Look,\" the blunt warnings, and the sarcastic jokes about how bad things go for half-bloods. Those choices make him sound like a kid talking to a friend, a kid who is also a little bit annoyed and a little bit scared."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 1–3 with a partner. Find two examples of informal or sarcastic word choice. For each, write the exact words in a two-column chart: left column, \"Words from the text\"; right column, \"What this shows about Percy's tone and first impression.\" Use at least one adverb or phrase telling how, when, or why in your explanation, such as \"bluntly,\" \"right away,\" or \"because he is afraid.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What words or phrases show the narrator's informal or sarcastic voice, and what first impression do they give you of Percy?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He starts with \"Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood,\" which sounds like someone talking, not a storyteller. The sarcastic warnings, like telling you to close the book, make him seem blunt and kind of grumpy, but also like he really cares about warning you."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy's comment about envying normal kids show about what he values, and what he fears?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He seems to value being normal and safe, because he envies kids who think this is just fiction. He fears the dangerous world of half-bloods, since he says it can get you killed."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.6"],"stem":"Which description best matches the tone of Percy's narration in the opening pages?","choices":[{"text":"Formal and scholarly, like a history textbook explaining an event","correct":false,"rationale":"The narrator uses casual phrases like \"Look,\" and speaks directly to the reader, which is the opposite of a formal textbook voice."},{"text":"Casual, blunt, and sarcastic, with a serious warning underneath","correct":true,"rationale":"Percy's informal voice and sarcastic comments sound like a kid talking, while his warnings show that he is serious about the danger."},{"text":"Cheerful and excited about discovering he is a half-blood","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses the adventure genre with Percy's attitude. He says he did not want to be a half-blood and calls it dangerous."},{"type":"x","text":"Calm and neutral, with no feelings about the events","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy shows strong feelings throughout, including envy, frustration, and fear, so his tone is not neutral."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students name tone and support it with specific words from the text.","sayAsk":"Offer a tone word bank: casual, blunt, sarcastic, serious, afraid, grumpy. Ask: Which word from the text makes you think that? Frames: The narrator sounds ___ because he says \"___.\" This word choice makes me think Percy is ___. Percy speaks ___ (bluntly / directly / honestly) when he says ___.","watchFor":"If students name a tone without citing words, then prompt: \"What exact words made you think that?\" If students copy a long passage, then have them choose the three most important words. Success: students quote a few words and explain the tone, using at least one adverb or phrase for detail (ELD.PII.6.5)."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: describing tone","tryThis":"Have students act out the line two ways, formal and casual, and describe the difference. Then choose a tone word from the bank and connect it to the exact words in the text."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite the opening warning in a formal voice and explain how the change in word choice would change the reader's first impression of Percy."}]}]},{"id":"lia-infer-predict","title":"Hero or Problem? Infer and Predict","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"teach","text":"hidden"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Readers make inferences by combining what the text says with what they already know. Then they use those inferences to predict. Notice that Percy narrates from the future, so he already knows how the story turns out. That is one reason his warnings feel so serious."},{"type":"directions","text":"Think quietly for one minute, then pair up and share. Use this chart: Evidence from pp. 1–8 | My inference about Percy | My prediction about his story. Choose at least two pieces of evidence, including one about how Percy is treated at school (trouble, expulsions, or punishments). Then answer: Is Percy being set up as a hero or a \"problem\" kid in a modern myth? Use the frame: Percy seems like a ___ because ___, so I predict ___."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What evidence from pp. 1–8 shows how adults and other kids see Percy? What does it make you infer about his place in the \"normal\" world?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The text says he has been expelled from schools and is on probation, so adults see him as a troublemaker. I infer that he doesn't fit in the normal world, even though he wants to."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Is Percy being set up as a hero or a problem figure? Which details point each way?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both. The trouble at school makes him look like a problem kid, but the narrator says he is a half-blood, which sounds like the special kind of person in myths. I predict the things people call problems will turn out to be signs he is a hero."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Based on these details, what big idea might the story be starting to build? Say it as an emerging theme, not a summary of what happened."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Maybe the theme is that people who don't seem normal might have special strengths. Percy is in trouble all the time, but that may be because he is meant for something else."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"This is an emerging theme only. Accept tentative wording such as \"maybe\" and \"might.\" The Performance Task skill for this lesson is identifying and explaining emerging themes. Use this activity to model the habit of linking details to a bigger idea. A fuller theme statement comes later in the unit."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students make and explain inferences and predictions using precise language and added details.","sayAsk":"Provide sentence frames and allow a partner rehearsal in the home language before English. Ask: What does the text say? What do you already know? What do you predict? Frames: The text says ___. I infer that ___ because ___. I predict that ___ will happen because ___. Percy is treated ___ (unfairly / harshly / like a troublemaker) at school.","watchFor":"If students state a prediction without evidence, then prompt: \"Which page or detail made you think that?\" If students retell the plot instead of inferring, then prompt: \"What does this detail suggest about Percy?\" Success: students connect a cited detail to an inference and a prediction in one complete explanation."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: moving from evidence to inference","tryThis":"Give a three-step frame: \"The text says ___. That makes me think ___. So I predict ___.\" Do the first row together using the expulsion detail."},{"type":"support-table-placeholder","tryThis":"remove"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to consider how a reader who believes Percy is a problem kid and a reader who believes he is a hero would each interpret the same detail, and explain which reading the evidence supports better."}]}]},{"id":"lia-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: Summary and Emerging Theme","minutes":4,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write 3 to 4 sentences. First, give a short summary of pp. 1–8 that sticks to what happens and what Percy says, with no opinions. Then add one sentence beginning \"An emerging theme might be...\" and support it with one detail from the text."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"A summary tells what the text says. It does not include whether you liked it or what you think about Percy. Your theme sentence is where your thinking begins, and it must be backed by evidence."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does a summary of these pages include that your opinion would not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A summary says Percy warns readers about being a half-blood, tells us he envies normal kids, and explains that he has been in trouble at school. An opinion would say he is annoying or cool. I keep the opinion out."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students write a short summary and theme sentence using added detail.","sayAsk":"Allow students to say their summary to a partner first. Frames: In pages 1–8, Percy tells readers that ___. At school, he ___. An emerging theme might be ___ because ___. Encourage adverbials: \"at his old schools,\" \"right at the start,\" \"because he feels different.\"","watchFor":"If students include opinion words like \"boring\" or \"cool,\" then prompt: \"Replace that with what the text says.\" If the theme sentence is only a plot detail, then prompt: \"What bigger idea does this detail point to?\" Success: students write a summary without opinion and a theme sentence tied to one detail."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: separating summary from opinion","tryThis":"Give two sample sentences and have students sort them into \"summary\" or \"opinion,\" then revise the opinion sentence into a summary sentence."},{"type":"support-table-end","tryThis":"remove"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a sentence that predicts how the theme might develop in the next section and cite the detail that supports the prediction."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on the evidence they found and connect today's thinking to the Performance Task and tomorrow's writing.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflection","title":"Exit Reflection","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the Performance Task, you will explain themes using evidence from stories. Today you took the first step: noticing details in Percy's own words and asking what bigger idea they might build. Tomorrow you will turn this evidence into a written explanation."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the sentence frame on your own: In the opening pages of The Lightning Thief, Percy's tone seems ___ because he says \"___.\" This suggests that he values ___ and fears ___. One word I learned today using word parts or context is ___, which means ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the opening pages of The Lightning Thief, Percy's tone seems blunt and sarcastic because he says \"Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood.\" This suggests that he values being normal and fears the dangerous half-blood world. One word I learned is immortal, which means not able to die, because im- means not and mort means death."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect the frames or scan them as students leave. Look for students who can name a tone, quote exact words, and state both a value and a fear. Use this to plan small groups for Lesson 5's writing."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Students keep reading and annotating, and meet a short fable that will connect to the unit's myth work.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-annotate","title":"Read and Annotate","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"1) Read and annotate Chapter 1 of The Lightning Thief, pp. 9–15. Mark one place where Percy's tone is informal or sarcastic, and one detail about how Percy is treated by others. 2) Read and annotate the excerpt from \"The Hare and the Lion.\" Mark one detail that shows how a character is described and one detail that might point to a lesson."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 9–15"},{"type":"text-reference","title":"\"The Hare and the Lion\" (excerpt)"}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students heard a fluent teacher read aloud of The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1 (pp. 1–8), and analyzed how Percy's informal, sarcastic narration creates tone and a first impression. They cited evidence to infer what Percy values and fears, predicted whether he is being set up as a hero or a problem figure, and recorded an emerging theme.","keyActivities":["Morphology word-building with mort-, -ology, and trans-, and adding ten vocabulary words to the Unit Vocabulary organizer","Teacher read aloud with think-alouds and in-context vocabulary verification (pp. 1–8)","Tone analysis annotation of informal and sarcastic word choices","Think-Pair-Share inferences and predictions about Percy as hero or problem figure","Quick Write: summary distinct from opinion plus an emerging theme"],"vocabularyTaught":["envy","recognize","frayed","expelled","probation","threatened","spawn","detention","immortal","dyslexia","mortal","mythology","transform","transport"],"standardsCovered":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","L.6.4","L.6.6","RL.6.4","RL.6.6","RL.6.10","ELD.PI.6.6","ELD.PI.6.7","ELD.PII.6.5"]}}
